Guigo
GWEE-goh
n. (c. 1083–1136, fifth prior of the Grande Chartreuse, author of the Customs of the Carthusians)
A Dauphinois form of the Germanic name Wido, wood or wide.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Guigo, usually called Guigo I to distinguish him from the later prior of the same name, governed the Grande Chartreuse from 1109 to 1136 and is the real organiser of the Carthusian order. Bruno had left no rule; Guigo was asked by other houses what the usage of the Chartreuse actually was, and about 1127 he wrote the Consuetudines Cartusiae, which fixed the solitary cell, the common office, the silence, the diet and the copying of books, and which the order has kept with remarkably little change for nine centuries. He also left a book of Meditations, short and unsparing. The ladder of four rungs that made the Carthusians famous, reading, meditation, prayer and contemplation, belongs to the later Guigo II. This dictionary records Guigo I for the care of books the Customs required, since he ordered every monk supplied with writing materials and told them they could preach with their hands what they could not preach with their mouths. Scripture puts the same weight on written witness, “Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it” (Hab 2:2), “What thou seest, write in a book” (Rev 1:11), and on reading that shapes a life, “in his law doth he meditate day and night” (Psa 1:2), “Thy word have I hid in mine heart, that I might not sin against thee” (Psa 119:11).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines custom as established practice; a prior as the superior of a convent; meditation as close or continued thought; to copy as to transcribe; and silence as forbearance of speech.

expand to see more

CUSTOM, n. Frequent or common use, or practice; a frequent repetition of the same act; established usage having the force of law.

PRIOR, n. The superior of a convent of monks, or one next in dignity to an abbot.

MEDITATION, n. Close or continued thought; the turning or revolving of a subject in the mind; serious contemplation.

COPY, v.t. To write, print or engrave according to an original; to form a like work by writing.

SILENCE, n. Forbearance of speech in man; taciturnity; omission of speech.

Key Scripture

Hab 2:2 — "And the LORD answered me, and said, Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it."

Rev 1:11 — "Saying, I am Alpha and Omega, the first and the last: and, What thou seest, write in a book, and send it unto the seven churches which are in Asia; unto Ephesus, and unto Smyrna, and unto Pergamos, and unto Thyatira, and unto Sardis, and unto Philadelphia, and unto Laodicea."

Psa 1:2 — "But his delight is in the law of the LORD; and in his law doth he meditate day and night."

Psa 119:11 — "Thy word have I hid in mine heart, that I might not sin against thee."

Modern Corruption

Fifth prior of the Grande Chartreuse, c. 1083–1136: wrote the Customs that still govern the order, and set every silent monk to copying books.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one Guigo put in the Customs: men vowed to silence were to preach with their hands. The copying of books was not a hobby of the cell but its public ministry. Scripture gives the practice its charter, “Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables” (Hab 2:2), and repeats the command to the last apostle, “What thou seest, write in a book” (Rev 1:11).

The second thing to keep is the discipline of continuous meditation, which the Carthusian day was built around. The psalms describe it without any mystical apparatus at all: a man delighting in the law and turning it over at all hours, “in his law doth he meditate day and night” (Psa 1:2), and storing it where it will do its work on him, “Thy word have I hid in mine heart, that I might not sin against thee” (Psa 119:11). The aim is not an experience but a changed man.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew kathab (H3789), to write; Greek grapho (G1125), to write; Hebrew hagah (H1897), to mutter, to meditate; Hebrew tsaphan (H6845), to hide away; Hebrew luach (H3871), a tablet.

expand to see more

Hebrew kathab (H3789) — to write, to set down plainly; “Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables”, Habakkuk 2:2.

Hebrew luach (H3871) — a tablet for a running reader; “that he may run that readeth it”, Habakkuk 2:2.

Greek grapho (G1125) — to write, by direct command; “What thou seest, write in a book”, Revelation 1:11.

Hebrew hagah (H1897) — to murmur, to muse continually; “in his law doth he meditate day and night”, Psalm 1:2.

Hebrew tsaphan (H6845) — to hide, to store up as treasure; “Thy word have I hid in mine heart”, Psalm 119:11.

Usage

"“Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables” (Hab 2:2) — the charter for a silent man with a pen."

"“in his law doth he meditate day and night” (Psa 1:2) — the Carthusian day, stated in a psalm."

"“that I might not sin against thee” (Psa 119:11) — what the storing is for."
